proof_review: An inclusion-minimal subfamily preserving all actual orbits loses some orbit connection when any mark is removed. One crossing transposition for each removed mark forms a forest, since every alternate selected-edge path avoids that mark. Parallel edges are also excluded. At least c components remain, giving at most d-c marks without any group-independence or quotient-IP premise.

At the unique crossing, any subfamily of the omission marks transitive on both A and B must contain every omission mark. Otherwise adjoining the crossing involution inside the omitted-label group connects the two transitive sides, contradicting that maximal omission being intransitive. The full crossing involution, not an asserted isolated pure transposition, suffices for this orbit argument.

For the two block actions, minimal transitivity requires at most m1+m2-2 marks on the disjoint union of the two block sets. Every actual point orbit of this subgroup meets all blocks of its side, so the numbers of point orbits are at most k1,k2. Every remaining eligible edge remains nonloop after contracting those actual orbits. Any contracted cycle lifts through those orbits to a path avoiding its own label; hence these remaining edges form a forest with at least two components. This proves the exact bound and the displayed (m-2)(k-2) arithmetic. No string relation or IP is used in this theorem.

For commuting H,K, K transports every specified H mark equivariantly between actual H-orbits. A subset transitive on one H-orbit is therefore transitive on all of them. Together with all K marks it is transitive on B and also A under the stated singleton-or-K-transitive alternative. Essentiality forces every H mark into that subset, giving p<=h-1. The symmetric block-orbit selection with all H marks gives q<=t-1. Both factors are nonempty, so h,t>=2, and h+t-2<=ht/2. No faithful restriction of either factor is inferred.

The singleton and two-point corollaries use the actual commuting left/right index intervals at an interior crossing. In the two-point case each interval contains its stated nontrivial adjacent restriction, so each is transitive there. Their bounds give exactly 2r<=n+1 and 2r<=n respectively.

In the strict range both sides cannot be imprimitive. A singleton at an interior index is excluded; a singleton at an endpoint gives the source-defined perfect split with an empty index side. Otherwise a nontrivial primitive side exists. If its active indices have a gap, the two images commute, are nontrivial normal subgroups of their primitive product, and are transitive. Centralizing a transitive permutation group makes every nonidentity active restriction fixed-point-free. The unique-crossing lemma then confines all active marks to the two neighbouring indices. Each factor is generated by one involution and is transitive, forcing degree two; the previously proved two-point corollary excludes it.

Thus the primitive active set is one interval avoiding the crossing index. Transitivity moves its anchor, and endpoint fixing confines such a moving mark to a neighbouring index, so the interval is adjacent. Reversal puts it on the right. If no mark is shared between sides, consecutive marks cannot change side without commuting and disconnecting the actual parent path. The right interval acts only on B and the left only on A, exactly the source definition of perfect split. Otherwise a shared mark must occur in the right-hand primitive interval.

The endpoint-fixing part of the acquired lemma requires the string relations and is used only in the final theorem, which states them. The revised introduction now says so explicitly. The generic forest and both-imprimitive arguments use only the unique-crossing two-orbit conclusion and actual omission intransitivity.
